strengths: MaskSub is a simple, technically coherent training modification: an unmasked supervised pass supplies detached targets to a masked pass sharing the same parameters. It adds no inference overhead and integrates naturally with established training recipes.

The central improvements are well supported. Table 1 reports gains of 0.3–0.7 percentage points across DeiT-III model sizes and training lengths. Three-run results in Table A.13 strengthen this evidence: ViT-B improves from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02.

The training-cost comparisons establish practical value beyond simply spending more computation. In Table 8, ViT-B with MaskSub achieves 84.1% using 25 GPU-days, versus 83.7% using 26 GPU-days for longer baseline training. Table 9 also shows better accuracy and lower cost than CoSub in the evaluated setting.

Evaluation is unusually broad, including pretrained-model finetuning, ResNet and Swin architectures, downstream classification, dense prediction, and robustness. Representative gains include ADE20K single-scale mIoU from 48.8 to 49.4 and ViT-B ImageNet-A accuracy from 36.8 to 41.9. These results support usefulness beyond the primary classification benchmark.

The appendix materially strengthens the submission. Table A.6 isolates the importance of distillation, while Tables A.7–A.8 examine masking ratios and loss weights. Algorithm 1 and Appendix B provide substantial implementation guidance. Overall, the supported practical contribution favors acceptance despite reservations about novelty and interpretation.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental. The method combines established asymmetric consistency/self-distillation with token dropping. In particular, the claimed distinction from UDA based on 'distillation' versus 'consistency' is not mathematically persuasive: with detached targets, Equation (3)'s cross-entropy has the same student gradient as forward KL divergence. The contribution is more convincingly established as an effective supervised adaptation than as a fundamentally new learning objective.

The explanation of 'automatic difficulty control' exceeds the evidence. Aggregate gradient norms and loss curves support improved optimization in the tested settings, but do not establish the claim that masking effectively applies only to successfully predicted samples. Every sample receives the distillation loss, including confidently incorrect predictions. Table A.7 also shows a substantial gain without masking, indicating that ordinary consistency effects contribute to the improvement.

Benefits have meaningful boundaries. In Table A.10, adding MaskSub during finetuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89 to 89.55. Section 4.2 states that CLIP finetuning achieves the same best-checkpoint performance as the baseline, despite improved final-epoch results. These findings qualify the broad claims of consistent improvement. Furthermore, ResNet and Swin require approximately twice the training computation because their masking retains spatial structure.

Some comparisons and smaller gains are less conclusive than the central ViT results. Table 6 mixes substantially different training recipes, so only its matched-recipe comparisons isolate the self-distillation method. The 0.1-point BEiTv2 improvements and small detection gains lack uncertainty estimates. These limitations weaken sweeping superiority claims, although they do not negate the larger, repeated improvements.

Presentation refinements are secondary: Table 7 labels both CIFAR columns 'CIFAR100', and Section 4's blanket statement that all experiments use 50% masking overlooks the 15% BERT setting. The beyond-vision experiments also provide less complete task-specific training detail than the main vision experiments.
